title: How To Frame Competition When You're Outgunned
excerptForBlog:
We ended Q1 with over 48 million global members, and topped $1 billion in quarterly streaming revenue. We had higher domestic net additions than in Q1 2013, growing international success, and a big hit with Season 2 of House of Cards.

International revenues currently amount to 25% of our total streaming revenue and we anticipate our international segment to eventually surpass our U.S. market, similar to other Internet firms. International contribution losses shrank by $22 million q/q, with losses more than halved on a y/y basis due to the strong growth in paid members. Our present international segment is on a path to achieve profitability this year. However, our substantial expansion into new European markets in the second half of 2014 will keep our expanded international segment at a net loss.

We compete for original series with many linear TV networks (CBS, FX, HBO, BBC, etc.) and several Internet firms (Amazon, Hulu, Microsoft, AOL, Yahoo, etc.). Our advantages against other Internet firms are our scale in video and our focus. Our advantages against linear TV networks are Internet on-demand consumption and targeted show marketing. A Morgan Stanley survey from March showed that 17% of respondents viewed Netflix as the service that offered the best original programming, second only to HBO, and ahead of Showtime and Starz. To have achieved this recognition in our second year of original content creation is exciting and we are optimistic about building on our initial success.

lessonTitle: How To Frame Competition When You're Outgunned
lessonBody:
## 1. Core Message
Netflix crossed 48 million members and $1 billion in quarterly streaming revenue. International is 25% of streaming revenue, losses are shrinking, and the segment is on track to profitability — except new European launches in H2 2014 will push it back into the red. In originals, a Morgan Stanley survey ranked Netflix #2 behind HBO, ahead of Showtime and Starz, in only its second year of original content.

## 2. What the Executive Is Really Thinking
This letter is a positioning exercise for investors. Netflix is sandwiched between two scary groups: established TV networks (HBO, FX, CBS, BBC) and deep-pocketed internet companies (Amazon, Hulu, Microsoft, AOL, Yahoo). Rather than hide that, the letter names them and then tells the reader exactly which two weapons Netflix uses against each side. It also pre-explains why international losses will get worse before they get better — pre-empting an obvious investor complaint about European expansion.

## 3. Key Management Lessons

### Name your competitors out loud
#### What it means
Netflix lists the rivals directly: CBS, FX, HBO, BBC on one side; Amazon, Hulu, Microsoft, AOL, Yahoo on the other.
#### Why it matters
Vague language about "the competitive landscape" lets investors imagine the worst. Naming names forces clarity and shows management has actually mapped the field.
#### MBA Perspective
This is Porter's Five Forces applied honestly — Netflix is identifying rivalry across two distinct competitor classes with different cost structures and business models.
#### Real-world application
In a board deck or fundraising memo, list your real competitors by name and group them by type. If you can't, you don't understand your market yet.

### Pick two advantages per opponent — no more
#### What it means
Against internet rivals: "scale in video and our focus." Against TV networks: "Internet on-demand consumption and targeted show marketing." Two each. That's it.
#### Why it matters
A long list of advantages signals confusion. Two clean ones force prioritization and are easy for investors, employees, and partners to remember.
#### MBA Perspective
Resource-Based View: durable advantage comes from a small number of resources that are valuable, rare, and hard to imitate. Scale and focus are both genuinely hard for Yahoo or Microsoft to replicate against a video-only company.
#### Real-world application
Write one sentence per major competitor explaining why you win. If you need more than 15 words, your edge isn't sharp enough.

### Use external proof, not self-praise
#### What it means
Netflix cites a Morgan Stanley survey showing 17% rank it #1 in originals, second to HBO.
#### Why it matters
Management saying "our shows are great" is worthless. A third-party number is harder to dismiss and anchors the claim.
#### MBA Perspective
This is brand equity measurement. Ranking second to HBO in year two of originals positions Netflix inside the premium category, not against generic streaming.
#### Real-world application
When pitching strength, lead with the survey, the NPS, the analyst quote, the customer logo — not your own adjective.

### Pre-explain bad news before investors find it
#### What it means
The letter says international is on track to profitability this year — then immediately says new European launches will keep the segment at a net loss.
#### Why it matters
Investors hate surprises more than losses. Telling them the loss is a choice (expansion) rather than a problem (weak demand) reframes a negative number as a strategic bet.
#### MBA Perspective
This is investment-phase signaling. Losses caused by growth spending are treated very differently from losses caused by operational decay.
#### Real-world application
When reporting a miss, separate "things we chose" from "things that happened to us." Take ownership of the first, explain the second.

### Set the long-term frame early
#### What it means
Netflix says international will "eventually surpass our U.S. market, similar to other Internet firms."
#### Why it matters
This single sentence reframes every future quarterly loss in Europe as a step toward a larger prize. It gives investors a ruler other than this quarter.
#### MBA Perspective
Analogical reasoning to set expectations: by pointing to "other Internet firms," Netflix borrows a pattern investors already believe (Google, Facebook, eBay all went majority-international) and applies it to itself.
#### Real-world application
Give your investors a long-term yardstick early. Then short-term pain reads as progress, not failure.

## 4. Strategic Analysis (MBA Style)

### Competitive Strategy
Netflix refuses to fight on one front. Against TV it competes on technology and personalization ("on-demand", "targeted show marketing"). Against internet rivals it competes on focus and scale. This is asymmetric — it picks a different battlefield for each enemy rather than trying to beat HBO at HBO's game or Amazon at Amazon's.

### Risk Analysis
Two risks are visible. First, originals: if Netflix can't produce hits, the only thing separating it from a generic catalog service disappears — hence the emphasis on the survey result. Second, international cash burn: European expansion is expensive, and the letter is managing investor patience in advance.

### Build vs Buy Analysis
The document doesn't discuss M&A. But the choice to build originals in-house (House of Cards Season 2 is named as a "big hit") rather than license content from the same networks Netflix now competes with is the implicit build decision. Licensing would have meant funding rivals.

### Market Dynamics
The competitor list reveals an industry where the line between "TV" and "internet" has dissolved. A streaming company now competes with both BBC and Yahoo. That's an unusual structure — most industries have one type of rival. Netflix's response is to claim it's the only player focused entirely on video at scale.

### Long-Term Strategic Implications
If the strategy works, Netflix becomes a global subscription platform larger internationally than domestically, with originals strong enough to keep churn low. If it fails, the European spend produces sub-scale country operations and the originals brand never reaches HBO's tier, leaving Netflix as a commoditized library competing on price.

## 5. Hidden Insights
- **Focus is being framed as a moat.** Saying "our focus" is an advantage against Amazon and Microsoft is really saying: those companies will never care about video as much as we do. That's a bet that conglomerates can't out-execute specialists.
- **HBO is the real target.** Being "second only to HBO" tells investors which company Netflix wants to be compared to — a premium brand, not a Hulu or a Yahoo.
- **The European loss is being pre-sold.** Mentioning profitability and then immediately taking it away is a careful sequence designed to lock in credit for the trajectory before announcing the spend.
- **"Similar to other Internet firms"** quietly reclassifies Netflix as a tech company, not a media company — which matters for the valuation multiple investors apply.
pullQuote: When you face bigger rivals on every side, define the game by the two things only you can do well.
